notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest number appearing on either side of a card that is not equal on the same card's front and back.
Idea: Collect numbers from both sides, excluding any number that appears on a card with identical front and back.
Technique and why it applies: A number shown identically on both sides can never be hidden by flipping that card, so it is disqualified. The minimum remaining number is the answer.
Invariant: The exclusion set contains all values for which front equals back on at least one card.
Edge cases: If every value is disqualified, the fallback [0] returns zero. The code repeatedly constructs the exclusion set inside the comprehension, which is inefficient.
Complexity: Set construction repeated per candidate can make runtime O(n²); auxiliary space is O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the smallest number that can be visible on a card after flipping, but never appears on both sides of the same card.
Idea: Build the set of numbers on cards with identical sides, then scan all front and back values for the minimum outside that set.
Technique and why it applies: Identical-sided cards cannot hide their value, so those values are forbidden. Any other value can be exposed by choosing the appropriate side.
Invariant: same contains every forbidden number, and result is the smallest eligible value seen.
Edge cases: If no eligible number exists, infinity remains and the method returns zero. The code assumes fronts and backs have equal length.
Complexity: Building the set and scanning both arrays take O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Count binary trees whose node values come from nums and where each non-leaf node equals the product of its children.
Idea: Memoize the number of trees rooted at each value, beginning with one single-node tree.
Technique and why it applies: For every factor pair in nums whose product is num, multiply the possible left and right subtree counts and add them. Ordered child choices are counted separately by iterating all factors.
Invariant: helper(num) counts all valid trees with root num.
Edge cases: nums is converted to a set, removing duplicates. The snippet uses lru_cache without importing it, so it needs that name externally.
Complexity: Each value scans all unique values, giving O(u²) factor checks plus recursion/cache work and O(u) cached states for u unique values.

Task and constraints: Count binary trees where each non-leaf value is the product of its two child values.
Idea: Sort values and build a DP count for each possible root value.
Technique and why it applies: Each smaller A[j] is considered as a left child; if it divides A[i] and the complementary factor has a DP count, their product gives the number of trees using that ordered pair.
Invariant: dp[x] counts valid trees rooted at value x using factors already processed.
Edge cases: Sorting ensures any factor smaller than the product has already been processed. The result is reduced modulo 10^9+7.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(n²) time and O(n) DP space.

Task and constraints: Convert each word in a sentence to Goat Latin.
Idea: Split the sentence on spaces and transform each word based on whether its first letter is a vowel.
Technique and why it applies: Vowel-starting words remain in place; other words move their first character to the end. Each word then receives ma followed by a number of a characters equal to its one-based word index.
Invariant: result contains transformed words in original order, separated by one space.
Edge cases: split(' ') preserves empty tokens from repeated spaces, which can lead to indexing an empty word and an error. The standard input uses single spaces between nonempty words.
Complexity: Repeated string concatenation can take O(n²) time; output storage is O(n).

Task and constraints: Transform a sentence into Goat Latin while preserving word order.
Idea: Split on whitespace, transform each word, and join the results with single spaces.
Technique and why it applies: A consonant-starting word moves its first letter to the end; every word receives ma plus a repeated a suffix based on its position.
Invariant: convert yields each transformed word in order, and join reconstructs the sentence.
Edge cases: split() collapses multiple spaces and ignores leading/trailing whitespace. The code assumes each word is nonempty.
Complexity: Processing and joining take O(n) time and O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Count directed friend requests between people based on age eligibility rules.
Idea: Count frequencies by age and sum the number of eligible ordered pairs of ages.
Technique and why it applies: request(a,b) implements the age predicate. The product c[a]*(c[b]-int(a==b)) counts distinct ordered people, excluding self-requests when ages are equal.
Invariant: c records how many people have each age.
Edge cases: The same-age case subtracts one from the available recipient count. The age predicate encodes the problem's restrictions on older/younger recipients.
Complexity: With U distinct ages, the double loop takes O(U²) time and the Counter uses O(U) space.

Task and constraints: Maximize total profit by assigning each worker at most one job whose difficulty does not exceed their ability.
Idea: Sort jobs by difficulty, build a prefix maximum profit, and binary-search the hardest feasible job for each worker.
Technique and why it applies: The prefix maximum ensures each difficulty threshold stores the best profit among all jobs no harder than it. Binary search finds the rightmost feasible threshold.
Invariant: arr[i][1] is the best profit available among jobs through difficulty arr[i][0].
Edge cases: bestProfit starts at zero, so a worker with no feasible job contributes zero. The code uses inf without importing or defining it, causing NameError at maximum initialization.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), prefix maxima O(n), and each of m workers searches in O(log n), giving O(n log n+m log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the largest island obtainable by changing at most one water cell to land.
Idea: Use DSU to label connected land components and store each component's size.
Technique and why it applies: Land neighbors are unioned, with rank used as component size. For each water cell, the sizes of distinct neighboring components are summed, then one is added for the flipped cell.
Invariant: rank[root] stores the size of a DSU component, and parent links represent connected land.
Edge cases: The code indexes cells with i*m+j instead of i*n+j; this is safe only for a square grid, as guaranteed by the problem. If the grid is all land, max(rank) returns its area.
Complexity: DSU construction is near O(mn α(mn)); checking each water cell examines four neighbors, for O(mn α(mn)) time and O(mn) space.

Task and constraints: Maximize island area after flipping at most one zero to one.
Idea: DFS-label each island with a unique integer, record its area, then test every zero by summing neighboring island areas.
Technique and why it applies: The set of adjacent labels prevents counting the same island more than once. Flipping a zero joins all distinct neighboring islands plus the new cell.
Invariant: grid cells above one identify their island, and area maps each label to its component size.
Edge cases: If there are no land cells, area is empty and result starts at zero; flipping any zero yields one. If there are no zeros, the largest existing island is returned.
Complexity: Each cell is visited once during labeling and once during the candidate scan, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) recursion/area storage.

Task and constraints: Sum the number of substrings in which each character contributes only when it appears exactly once.
Idea: Record occurrence indices for each character and count the substrings in which each occurrence is unique.
Technique and why it applies: For occurrence i, left is the distance from the previous same character (or start boundary), and right is the distance to the next occurrence (or end boundary). Their product counts substrings where this occurrence is the sole copy.
Invariant: idx_recorder[c] stores the sorted positions of character c.
Edge cases: The code uses collections.defaultdict without importing collections, so it needs that name externally. Empty strings return zero.
Complexity: Building positions is O(n); summing contributions is O(n), with O(n) storage.

Task and constraints: Count unique-character contributions over all substrings, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: For each character occurrence, use its previous two positions and next occurrence to compute how many substrings it uniquely contributes to.
Technique and why it applies: The contribution is (i-j)*(j-k), where j is the current occurrence and k is the previous previous occurrence. A final pass accounts for substrings extending to the end.
Invariant: index[c] stores the previous two positions of each uppercase character.
Edge cases: The code assumes the alphabet is uppercase A-Z because it initializes string.ascii_uppercase keys. Contributions are reduced modulo MOD.
Complexity: Two linear passes take O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed alphabet.

Task and constraints: Count ways to express positive integer n as a sum of consecutive positive integers.
Idea: Increase the sequence length i and maintain the minimum offset csum=i(i-1)/2.
Technique and why it applies: A length-i sequence starting at x sums to i*x+csum. It is valid exactly when n-csum is divisible by i and csum<n.
Invariant: csum is the sum of offsets 0 through i-1 for the current length i.
Edge cases: n is positive; the loop stops once csum reaches n because no positive starting value can then work.
Complexity: The loop runs O(n) iterations and uses O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the start and end indices of every run of at least three identical adjacent characters.
Idea: Track the current run length and append its interval when the character changes or the string ends.
Technique and why it applies: When a new character differs, the previous run ends at i-1 and starts at i-c. The final-character branch appends a run that reaches the end.
Invariant: c is the length of the current run, and prev is its character.
Edge cases: The bitwise & combines two boolean conditions at the final position; it works here but logical and would be clearer. Empty input returns an empty list.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond output.

Task and constraints: Find all intervals of at least three equal consecutive characters.
Idea: Scan each position and close a group whenever the current character differs from the next character or the string ends.
Technique and why it applies: The boundary j marks the end of a run beginning at i. If its length j-i+1 is at least three, the interval is appended and i advances to the next group.
Invariant: i is the start of the current run, and j scans through it.
Edge cases: The end-of-string condition ensures the last group is checked. Empty input returns an empty list.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond output.

Task and constraints: Mask personal information, using an email-specific mask or a phone-number mask.
Idea: For emails, reveal the first and last local-part letters and lowercase the domain; for phone numbers, retain the last four digits and mask preceding digits.
Technique and why it applies: Email formatting inserts five stars between the local-part endpoints. Phone formatting strips punctuation while building the masked number and prepends a country-code mask based on extra digits.
Invariant: res accumulates the formatted output, and l tracks local phone digits processed.
Edge cases: The email branch assumes exactly two domain labels and can fail for domains with additional dots. The phone branch uses intricate length-based conditions, so unusual formatting should be checked carefully.
Complexity: Both branches scan the input once, giving O(n) time and O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Reverse each row of a binary image and invert every bit.
Idea: Reverse each row with slicing and replace each bit b by 1-b.
Technique and why it applies: Reversing changes horizontal order; subtracting each bit from one flips zero to one and one to zero.
Invariant: Every output row is the inversion of the corresponding reversed input row.
Edge cases: Empty rows remain empty. The method creates new rows and does not mutate the input.
Complexity: Each cell is processed once, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) output space.

Task and constraints: Flip each row horizontally and invert its binary values in place.
Idea: Swap symmetric positions while XORing both values with one.
Technique and why it applies: XOR with one toggles a binary bit. Swapping the toggled values reverses the row while inverting it; the middle element of an odd-length row is toggled once.
Invariant: After each iteration, the processed outer pairs are correctly reversed and inverted.
Edge cases: The loop uses (len(row)+1)//2, so the center element is processed for odd lengths. The input matrix is modified in place.
Complexity: Each row uses O(length) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Apply multiple source-to-target replacements to a string only when each source matches at its original index.
Idea: Sort replacement operations by index and adjust later indices by the net length change from earlier replacements.
Technique and why it applies: offset tracks cumulative length difference. Before applying a replacement, the code checks the source substring at the adjusted index; if it matches, it replaces it and updates offset.
Invariant: s reflects all successful earlier replacements, and offset is the total length change from those replacements.
Edge cases: Debug print statements run for failed matches. The approach assumes replacement indices refer to the original string and do not overlap in a conflicting way.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(k log k); repeated slicing/rebuilding can take O(k·n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Replace substrings at specified original indices when the source text matches.
Idea: Process operations in descending index order so replacements to the right cannot shift positions to the left.
Technique and why it applies: Each source is checked against S[i:i+len(s)]; only exact matches are replaced. Reverse ordering preserves the original indices for remaining operations.
Invariant: Before each operation, all edits are to the right of its index, so the prefix through i is unchanged.
Edge cases: Mismatched sources are ignored. The code returns a new string and does not mutate the original S object.
Complexity: Sorting is O(k log k), and repeated string slicing can cost O(k·n) time and O(n) space.
